Now what we have to do is allocate these courses to the teachers.
Obviously each course is going to be taught by exactly one teacher.
But also we would like that each teacher teaches only one course.
And that course should be something that the teacher is willing to teach.
So we would not like an allocation for example,

So we want to find some kind of allocation that each course is taught by a single instructor.
Each instructor teaches only one course.

So this is what is called a matching problem.
In particular it's called bipartite matching.
So what is a bipartite graph?
A bipartite graph is in which one in which the vertices come in two groups,
which we call B0 and B1.
And all the edges go from B0 to B1.
So there are no edges inside B0, there are no edges inside B1.
So this is the example here.
So this for example the teachers are B0 and the courses are B1.
Now there are no edges between courses, there are no edges between teachers.
All the edges are from a teacher to a course.
Now what we have asked is to find an allocation.

So here is how we can answer this question using network flows.
We add a spurious source node feeding into the teachers.

So this is a general example of what we call a reduction.
So we want to solve a given problem, problem A.

So in this last couple of lectures what we have seen are two what I would call big hammers.
So we have linear programming and network flows.
We actually express network flows in terms of linear program but network flows independently
are a very powerful modeling formula.
So many algorithm problems can actually be reduced to one of these two.
Either you can set up variables and set up a linear program or you can take a graph
of the analytic problem and model it using flows.
And the nice thing about this is that linear programming and network flows are both a very
standard problem for which people have invested a lot of time to write general purpose tools
which solve these problems.
So you can set up an arbitrary linear program, arbitrary network flow, give it to the tool
to give you an answer.
So you have efficient off the shelf implementations.
So in many practical situations rather than try and solve an algorithmic problem directly
it does often make sense to think of whether it can be modeled as a linear program or
a network flow and then use an off the shelf package to solve it.
But of course you have to be able to express the problem in terms of one of these things.
So in order to understand whether you can do so or not you need to spend some time analyzing
what can and cannot be expressed as linear programs.
In linear programs the crucial thing is that the constraints must be linear functions.
Sometimes you have constraints which refer to the product or two variables.
This is not a linear function.
Similarly network flows you have to make sure that you can actually model it as a source
to target flow.
You cannot be something going around a normal network.
So within these constraints however both of these are extremely useful generic problems
for which efficient solutions do exist and which can be exploited in a large number of
situations to solve the given problem at hand.
